title: Afa
description: Divination, and how it is read.
html:
Read in the Ide dialect. The original is written in Igbo; here the one term that changes is chi → si, Ide has chi: it is the word, and si / sị is how it is widely said. Nothing here is rewritten — the documents stand as written.

Afa

The divination system of Odiana: what it is, what is used, and exactly how a reading is done.

afa is the middle pillar of the religion. Ana is the law, the community and the spirits enforce it, and afa is how the divine will is known. The doctrine is that Agwu reveals through afa — not that afa is Agwu — and everything below follows from that.

The account here is the old order's. The apparatus, the session, the throw, the reading and the rule of interpretation are all as the the old order material describes them, and where another Igbo source adds something it is marked.

1 · What afa is

afa is a binary system of signs cast with a pair of chaplets and read as pairs of words, which the diviner then builds into sentences. It answers a question put to it, and it is expected to answer that question and not another — §10 is the rule that enforces it.

Every sign has a name and a meaning, and the meanings combine. The diviner's work is not to read one throw but to follow a thread: he asks, throws, reads, asks the next question from what he read, and throws again. A session is a conversation, not a single cast.

2 · The apparatus

The chaplets

"The major instrument used in communication with agwu is a pair of chaplets. Each chaplet is a

continuous string of four broad beads separated by four beads of cylindrical bones from the spines of

fish."

Four seeds to a chaplet, and two chaplets, one held in each hand.

Each seed has a concave side and a convex side. On landing it shows one or the other, and that is the whole of the signal:

| the seed lies | is read | |---|---| | concave side up, convex side down | OPEN | | convex side up, concave side down | CLOSED |

Four seeds give sixteen dispositions — 2⁴ — and two chaplets thrown together give 16 × 16 = 256, read at the intersection.

(A second Igbo account describes the chaplet as four discs of ujuru fruit, and names the two poles: all four closed is akwu, all four open is obi. Both accounts agree on the binary; they differ on what the beads are made of.)

The diviner's kit, laid out before a session

"Before an afa session, the afa man will place on the ground before him":

| item | what it is for | |---|---| | the image of agwu, with all or some of its household and its associated animals | the presence the diviner speaks with | | a small water vessel | "with which to threaten agwu if it begins to play pranks by lying" | | white chalk, nzu | specially prepared, for making marks on the ground | | a horn | "used by the afa man to blow off bad talk or signs from agwu" | | the diviner's ofo | "a symbol of his authority… handed to him as a consecrated staff, obtained from the olo tree, on the day he completed his training as a dibia afa" |

And all of it, apart from the images, is carried in an empty tortoise shell — the tortoise being the animal of the folktales.

3 · Who may divine

Only a dibia afa — a diviner who has completed the training and holds the ofo.

The ofo is the licence. It is "handed to him as a consecrated staff, obtained from the olo tree, on the day he completed his training" — so a person does not become a diviner by deciding to be one, and the instrument of his office is given at the end of his training and not before.

And a diviner does not talk. The tradition's own prohibition: a dibia afa must not speak openly about what he reads.

The training is long, and the tradition's own account puts it in decades: a man spends about fifteen years to qualify, and twenty more before he is respected as a master. What he learns:

  • the sixteen signs, and their names;
  • the 256 combinations, and how they are read at the intersection;
  • the afa vocabulary — the words each disposition carries, and the compounds;
  • the grammar of the language — which combinations are meaningful and which are not;
  • the praise songs and the proverbs used in a session, because the diviner speaks in both.

4 · Preparing a session

The order is fixed, and it is taken from a session recorded on 10 August 1976 — an elder of a lineage and five of his relations came to a diviner, and the account runs from the first greeting to the last word.

| # | what is done | |---|---| | 1 | the clients are received in the temple — the diviner receives them "in his temple", and this is a room, not a field | | 2 | kola is offered and shared. "The afa man offered kolanut which was shared by the dibia" | | 3 | the diviner calls on Chukwu to send his blessing, and obliquely refers to the reason his clients have come — he does not make them state it first | | 4 | a light conversation follows, until the eldest of the clients interrupts and states the purpose of the visit | | 5 | the offering is placed. The client "paid a little token fee" — in the recorded session, thirty kobo "for kolanut" — and places it on the floor before the diviner | | 6 | the diviner blows his horn | | 7 | white chalk is given, and the diviner makes four vertical parallel marks on the ground with it | | 8 | he takes up the pair of chaplets, and the reading begins |

Nothing is killed at any point in a reading, and nothing is poured out — the reading is free: nothing is charged for it, and the offering is not a fee, and the chalk is a marking and not a sacrifice.

5 · How a reading is made

The method is a loop, and it is the whole of the system:

the diviner asks a question → he throws the pair → he reads the pair → he says what it means → the

meaning raises the next question, and he throws again.

He does not throw once and interpret for an hour. He throws twenty times or more, each throw answering the question he asked before it, and each answer drawing the next question out of him.

The throw

One chaplet in each hand, thrown forward so that they come to rest parallel to one another. The four seeds of each chaplet show open or closed as they fall.

And the fall is not perfectly random — the source is explicit: the seeds "are slightly different in weight and shape and therefore non-symmetrical", so "the law of probability" applies less cleanly than it would to coins, and "the skill of the dibia afa in throwing may tend to vary the probability." The diviner's hand is part of the instrument, and the tradition says so.

The read

The two chaplets are read together, and the words are read right to left — "not like conventional reading which is from left to right": B-A-T reads as 'tab'.

So one throw gives a pair of afa words, and the pair is the statement. From the recorded session: a throw reading Ofu Ijite, Aghali Okala is given as "the worthless talk of an ozo titled man." Two words, one sentence.

6 · The sixteen signs

| sign | what it carries | |---|---| | Akwu | the zero of the system; stillness — all four seeds closed | | Obi | one; motion — all four seeds open | | Ofu / Okala | the single, the one; and Ofu Ijite reads as worthless talk | | Ijite / Ogwute | I-am-ness; being, presence | | Aghali | strength, will, victory — the sign of Ikenga; Aghali Okala reads as an ozo titled man | | Ete | — | | Ose | the opened eye | | Aka | journey, motion | | Atulukpa | things tied, things wrapped — sacred structure and disciplined distinction | | Obala | making hidden things visible | | Oha | the assembly, the people | | Ora | illumination, fire, truth | | Odii | midnight | | Ogoli / Ogholi | — Odi Ogoli reads as a supernatural being | | Otule | okwu and ikpe — speech, disputes, judgment | | Ululu | gravity, anchoring, burden, consequence |

Eight of these are attested in two independent sources, which is a stronger footing than the rest: Aka journey, Aghali = Ikenga, Akwu stillness, Atulukpa things tied, Odii midnight, Ose the opened eye, Otule = okwu/ikpe, Ululu gravity.

And one is exact: Ululu is "gravity, anchoring, burden", which is precisely the religion's own teaching on spiritual debt — "something heavy… something that anchors… bound to gravity."

7 · The 256, and how they are read

Sixteen dispositions to a chaplet, two chaplets, 16 × 16 = 256. Both Igbo sources reach the number and they reach it differently: one by combination — "the sixteen signs are combined into 256 pairs" — and the other by vocabulary — "the whole asusu afa has 256 words as its total vocabulary." The number is the system's size, whether it is counted as pairs or as words.

The table

The combinations are written as a table of sixteen blocks of sixteen cells. Each block is headed by its own cell, and the headings are compounded with NABO — and NABO has a rule:

"Nabo is substituted where otherwise there would be a repetition."

So where a combination would repeat, NABO stands in for it — which is how the table stays sixteen by sixteen without collisions.

About 150 of the 256 cells survive in the sources. Roughly a hundred do not, and that gap is the author's — it is the one thing the religion cannot supply from what it has.

And the words compound

An afa word is built from its signs, and the order matters. The code language has a real grammar:

  • ogoli-ete means belly — but ete-ogholi means a bush. The same two signs, reversed, are

two different words.

  • Some combinations are simply wrong. "It is therefore ungrammatical and meaningless in the afa

language to say ogholi-ete or ete-ogoli, or ogwute-aka instead of ijite-aka, or aka-ijite instead of aka-ogwute."

  • Each sign has a feminine form, used when it follows rather than leads: ayali before,

ogwute after, and so on through the set.

  • And some pairs are simply memorised: "There is no rule about those ones. You only need to memorise

them."

8 · The session, as it actually runs

From the recorded session of 10 August 1976. A family came about trouble — "frequent quarrels, illness and mishaps" — and this is what the diviner did, throw by throw:

| throw | the question, and the words | what it meant | |---|---|---| | 1 | "What is it?" | mischief | | 2 | "What mischief?" | — | | 3 | "Against whom?" — followed by a proverb | — | | 4 | "Which Ogugu?" — and he recites a praise song to Ogugu | a supernatural being called Ogugu | | 5 | "What type of gun shot?" | — | | … | "Do what, or give what?" · "Why trouble?" (twice, with a proverb) | — | | 12 | Odi Orunukpa | the mother's lineage | | 13 | Aka Akwu | the ancestors | | 14 | Ijite Aghali | make a blood sacrifice | | 15 | Obala Akwu | coming with worthless talk | | 16–17 | "Who puts trouble aside?" · "Why trouble?" · "Blackmail?" · "Okay! But what do you want?" (with a proverb) | — | | 18–21 | all repetitions of the seventeenth throw | — | | end | "Agwu! Say something!" — and he recites a praise song to Agwu | the verdict |

And the verdict, in the diviner's own words: "afa is ended. Agwu is angry because your people have been erring for long. They turned deaf ears to all warnings." — then he stopped.

Two things in that are the whole method. The diviner speaks to Agwu aloud and recites to him before he delivers the answer. And he stops when he is done — there is no padding, and no second reading to soften the first.

9 · The examples the sources record

Case: a man suddenly successful. A man from a nearby village had been "dramatically successful in his business in the past two years", and he and his relations came anxious — "Will this good fortune continue? Can it be kept going? Are some people not becoming jealous?" The diviner assured them things were and would be fine, but warned that he must support the mayo — the village age-grade — for after all, he owed his success to the village and his ancestors. The man "delighted, felt relaxed."

Case: naming a child. A wife had delivered a male child. "The child must be a re-incarnate of one of the successful ancestors, whose name the child should bear." The naming ceremony was due, and the diviner was consulted to find out which of the ancestors had reincarnated in the child. — So afa is not only for trouble: it is what tells a family whose name a new child carries.

And the sessions at the palace. Cases were handled "at the the old order palace and at the lineage", and major abominations were brought to court — so afa served the law as well as the household.

10 · How a reading is judged — the rule that makes it falsifiable

This is the most important rule in the system, and it is what keeps a diviner honest.

1. Every sign carries a dominant theme. 2. The diviner checks whether the themes he has thrown match the theme of the question he was asked. 3. A mismatch means Agwu is lying — and it is cured, not ignored: the diviner blows his horn and sings praises to Agwu for lying, "and employs it to stop lying." 4. And if it keeps lying, the session ends.

"If the afa throws continue to be out of tune with the client's main theme of enquiry, the predictor

generally abandons his efforts and pleads with his client to come back another day."

So a reading that does not answer the question is not a reading, and the diviner says so. No session is stretched to fit, no answer is manufactured out of a bad cast, and the client goes home and comes back another day.

That rule is why afa can be trusted as far as it goes, and Odiana states it as the diviner's standing obligation.

11 · What afa is used for

| the question | who comes | |---|---| | illness, quarrels and misfortune in a family | the household, with its elders | | whether good fortune will hold | the successful, and their relations | | which ancestor a new child carries | the parents, before the naming | | an abomination, and what it requires | the lineage, and the court | | before war, a journey, or a founding | the ward and the town | | the state of the land | the priest, before a cleansing |

And what it is not for. It is not a lottery, and it is not consulted twice for the same question to get a better answer — the second reading is the one that lies.

And on a moral question the signs show imbalance, and never guilt. When afa is consulted about a wrong — a quarrel, a harm, an obligation broken — the reading may point to deceit, injustice, harmful conduct, an unresolved conflict, or the need for cleansing. It points; it does not convict. The diviner reads the signs alongside the facts of the matter — the ground, the witnesses, the accounts of the people — and where the wrong is established the remedy is repair rather than punishment: the harm corrected, the relationship restored, and the person or the community returned to balance by confession, restitution, reconciliation and cleansing.

Afa reveals imbalance. Truth establishes the wrong. Justice corrects it. Purification restores harmony. And so afa may never be used to convict a person — a community that takes a sign for a verdict has abandoned the ground and the witnesses, and has used the sign to do the very thing it exists to uncover.

12 · What Odiana adds, and what it owes the author

Odiana performs afa as the sources describe it: the same pair of chaplets, the same open and closed, the same right-to-left pairing, the same question-and-throw loop, the same scrutiny of whether the reading answers the question, and the same ending — the praise to Agwu and the verdict.

Reformed: the blood sacrifice. In the recorded session a throw read Ijite Aghali and the prescription was "make a blood sacrifice." In Odiana it is not. The reading stands; the remedy is the oblation — kola, nzu, palm wine, and a cleansing — and the amendment is registered in canon.md.

And the words of the session are Odiana's. The sources give the method and the exchanges of a real session; they do not give a liturgy. The invocations are composed and are marked composed.

What the religion still needs from the author:

| gap | what it is | |---|---| | about a hundred cells | the combinations that did not survive | | the full disposition-to-name table | which disposition yields which word — §7 | | the afa vocabulary in full | the compounds, beyond the set the sources list | | the praise songs | the songs to Agwu and to the named beings, which a session recites | | the training | whether Odiana keeps the decades-long training, or sets its own |

The blood ruling, in one place

(The ruling is canon.md A11, and it is the same in every document of this religion.)

An animal is killed at every festival of Odiana and at every serious rite of it. The announcing of the year, the cleansing of a great abomination, the taking of a title, the consecration of a Dibia, the setting of a boundary, the burial of a head, the making of peace, and the opening of a war. The animal is killed in the open, and its blood is spilled upon open ground, away from every holy thing.

And no blood is brought to a shrine, or to an altar, or to a sacred object, or to a tree that is held sacred. Nothing holy in this religion is ever touched with blood. The altar keeps the kola, and the nzu, and the wine, and the water. This is a modernisation of Odinana and it is iwu — made, and published, and dated — and it is not a custom recovered from the ancestors.

What remains bloodless, and stays bloodless:

  • the offering to Chukwu — the tradition's own offering was kola, white chalk and libation, and it is kept;
  • the household shrine — the household oblation is kola, nzu, mmanya and water;
  • the temple altar — no blood is brought to it, ever;
  • the consecration of objects — no shrine, Ofo, Ikenga or medicine is made with blood (canon.md A6);
  • a reading of afa — the reading is free: nothing is charged for it, and the offering is not a fee.

And the one blood that is never shed in this religion, in any rite and for any purpose, is human blood. Where the old practice used a human being, this religion uses the fowl — for it is the fowl that is used in performing sacrifice, and not a human being.
